subject: geography
title: US Middle School Geography - Landforms and Plate Tectonics Reading
subtitle: Reading passages and comprehension questions on tectonic landforms, hazards, and planning
description: Reading comprehension passages for a source-faithful geography pack on landforms and plate tectonics.

data.sourcePassage: Earth's outer layer is not one smooth shell. It is broken into large tectonic plates made of crust and uppermost mantle. These plates move slowly over the hotter, softer asthenosphere. The movement is usually only a few centimetres each year, but over millions of years it can build mountains, open ocean basins, create rift valleys, and trigger earthquakes. Heat inside Earth helps drive this movement as warmer mantle material rises, cools, and sinks. Plate tectonics also helps explain why many volcanoes and earthquakes form in lines or clusters instead of appearing randomly across the planet.

questions.question: What are tectonic plates made of?
questions.modelAnswer: They are made of crust and uppermost mantle.

questions.question: How fast do plates usually move?
questions.modelAnswer: They usually move only a few centimetres each year.

questions.question: Why can very slow plate movement still create major landforms?
questions.modelAnswer: Plates are enormous and move over millions of years, so small yearly movement can build mountains, rifts, and ocean basins.

questions.question: What pattern does plate tectonics help explain?
questions.modelAnswer: It explains why many earthquakes and volcanoes appear in lines or clusters near plate boundaries.

questions.question: Explain how mantle movement is connected to plate movement.
questions.modelAnswer: Warm mantle material rises, cools, and sinks, and this slow circulation helps move plates above the asthenosphere.

data.sourcePassage: The three main plate boundary types are divergent, convergent, and transform. At a divergent boundary, plates move apart. Magma rises into the gap and can create new crust, forming mid-ocean ridges under the sea or rift valleys on land. At a convergent boundary, plates move towards each other. Oceanic crust may subduct beneath another plate, producing trenches, volcanoes, and earthquakes. When two continental plates collide, crust crumples upward into high mountains such as the Himalayas. At a transform boundary, plates slide past each other. These boundaries usually do not create volcanoes, but they can cause strong earthquakes along faults.

questions.question: Which boundary type creates new crust as plates move apart?
questions.modelAnswer: A divergent boundary creates new crust.

questions.question: Which landform is linked to continental collision in the passage?
questions.modelAnswer: The Himalayas are linked to continental collision.

questions.question: Compare convergent and transform boundaries.
questions.modelAnswer: Convergent boundaries involve plates moving together and can create subduction, mountains, trenches, and volcanoes. Transform boundaries involve plates sliding past and mainly cause earthquakes.

questions.question: Why are transform boundaries usually not linked to volcanoes?
questions.modelAnswer: They usually do not involve subduction or magma rising into a gap, so volcano formation is uncommon.

questions.question: How does crust type affect what happens at a convergent boundary?
questions.modelAnswer: Dense oceanic crust can sink beneath another plate, while continental crust is less dense and tends to crumple upward into mountains.

data.sourcePassage: Tectonic regions can be dangerous, but they can also provide resources. Volcanoes can produce lava flows, ash fall, pyroclastic flows, lahars, gases, and landslides. Earthquakes can cause shaking, building collapse, fires, liquefaction, landslides, and tsunamis. However, volcanic areas may also provide fertile soils, geothermal energy, tourism, minerals, and new land. The impact of a hazard depends on both physical and human factors. Strong building codes, warning systems, public education, evacuation routes, and emergency planning can reduce risk. Weak buildings, poverty, limited emergency services, and high population density can make disasters worse.

questions.question: Which is listed as a volcanic benefit?
questions.modelAnswer: Geothermal energy is listed as a volcanic benefit.

questions.question: Which factor can make a disaster worse?
questions.modelAnswer: Weak buildings can make a disaster worse.

questions.question: Give one earthquake hazard and one volcanic hazard from the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: An earthquake can cause liquefaction, while a volcano can cause ash fall or a lahar.

questions.question: Why is a hazard not always the same as a disaster?
questions.modelAnswer: A hazard becomes a disaster when vulnerable people, buildings, and services are badly affected.

questions.question: Explain how a community can use resources while reducing tectonic risk.
questions.modelAnswer: It can use fertile soils or geothermal energy while planning evacuation routes, enforcing building codes, and educating people about hazards.

data.sourcePassage: Several places show how plate tectonics shapes land and human life. Japan lies near several plate boundaries and experiences earthquakes, volcanoes, and tsunamis, so it invests in drills, building codes, and warning systems. Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and is also influenced by volcanic activity, giving it geothermal energy, geysers, and eruption hazards. The Himalayas formed as the Indian Plate collided with the Eurasian Plate, creating the highest mountain range on Earth and important water sources. California is linked to transform movement along the San Andreas Fault. Haiti's 2010 earthquake showed how vulnerability can turn a hazard into a severe disaster.

questions.question: Which country uses geothermal energy linked to tectonic activity?
questions.modelAnswer: Iceland uses geothermal energy linked to tectonic activity.

questions.question: Which fault is linked to California?
questions.modelAnswer: The San Andreas Fault is linked to California.

questions.question: How are Japan and Iceland similar and different?
questions.modelAnswer: Both have tectonic hazards and volcanoes, but Japan is strongly linked to subduction while Iceland is linked to a divergent ridge and volcanic activity.

questions.question: Why are the Himalayas important for people beyond their height?
questions.modelAnswer: They store snow and glaciers that feed major rivers and influence climate, travel, tourism, and hazard risk.

questions.question: What does the Haiti example show about vulnerability?
questions.modelAnswer: It shows that weak infrastructure, poverty, limited emergency services, and crowded areas can make earthquake impacts much worse.

data.sourcePassage: Geographers use maps, data tables, graphs, and field evidence to understand tectonic patterns. A world map of earthquakes and volcanoes often shows lines around plate boundaries, especially around the Pacific Ring of Fire. A data table can compare regions by tectonic setting, hazards, resources, and human challenges. Climate graphs can show how elevation affects places such as Quito in the Andes, where temperatures stay mild because the city is high above sea level. Communities use this evidence to plan safer choices, such as avoiding the most dangerous zones, designing stronger bridges, preparing evacuation routes, and balancing resources with sustainability.

questions.question: Which region is especially known for a ring-like pattern of earthquakes and volcanoes?
questions.modelAnswer: The Pacific Ring of Fire is known for that pattern.

questions.question: Why does Quito have mild temperatures despite being near the Equator?
questions.modelAnswer: Its high elevation helps keep temperatures mild.

questions.question: How can data tables help geographers compare tectonic regions?
questions.modelAnswer: They can compare tectonic setting, hazards, resources, and human challenges across different places.

questions.question: Name two planning choices communities can make using hazard evidence.
questions.modelAnswer: Communities can avoid dangerous zones and design stronger bridges or evacuation routes.

questions.question: Explain why maps are useful but do not remove tectonic risk.
questions.modelAnswer: Maps show patterns and risk areas, but they cannot stop plate movement, so communities still need preparation and safer design.
